principles: Reuse the existing config-normalization logic (configuredValidationCommands) rather than re-implementing validate.commands[] parsing a second time
Mirror the semantics resolveCommandTimeoutMs already uses for lattice validate so both execution paths agree on the same command's effective timeout
No behavior change for commands with no configured override: the 270s default must stay exactly as-is
No circular import between core/validation-executor.ts and handlers/verifier.ts
Matching must not silently cross-match a different command that merely shares an executable
drivers: Cannot modify the lattice validate execution path or its default-ceiling semantics (excludedScope)
Cannot introduce a circular import between validation-executor.ts and verifier.ts (flagged by INIT review)
Fix must generalize beyond quorum-submit-smoke.js to any current or future validate.commands[] entry with a raised timeoutMs

options.name: checklist-layer-lookup
pros: No circular import: checklist.ts already depends one-way on both validation-executor.ts and verifier.ts, and is imported by neither
A single shared helper reused at all 4 existing call sites avoids duplicating the matching logic four times
runSingleAllowlistedCommand's own signature and behavior for any other caller stays exactly as documented (options.timeoutMs still wins when explicitly passed)
cons: Any future caller of runSingleAllowlistedCommand outside checklist.ts must remember to do the same lookup+pass rather than getting it automatically
Splits 'resolve a pinned command's effective timeout' logic across two files: matching in checklist.ts, floor/clamping in validation-executor.ts's resolveCommandTimeoutMs

options.name: executor-layer-lazy-import
pros: Every current and future caller of runSingleAllowlistedCommand gets the fix automatically with no call-site changes
Keeps all 'resolve a command's effective timeout' logic in one file (validation-executor.ts)
cons: A dynamic import() to dodge a same-package circular dependency is a workaround for a design smell, not a real fix, and can behave surprisingly under bundlers/tree-shaking
Still a de-facto circular dependency at the module-graph level even without a static deadlock - exactly what the INIT reviewer flagged as worth avoiding

rationale: Avoids the circular import outright instead of working around it with a lazy import; matches the alternative the INIT reviewer's own finding already named; centralizes the {executable,args} matching behind one shared helper called from all 4 existing checklist.ts call sites, and keeps validation-executor.ts's resolveCommandTimeoutMs untouched as required by scope-boundary.json. Matching key is strict {command,args} array equality (not label): label is cosmetic/user-facing text that can be renamed independent of the actual command, and args-based disambiguation is exactly what CHK-003's regression coverage already targets. configuredValidationCommands(root) is called fresh inside the shared helper on each invocation rather than cached/threaded from elsewhere - a single small local JSON read is negligible next to the command execution itself, and avoids adding cache-invalidation complexity this story does not need.

preMortem.scenario: The new helper matches by parsed {executable,args} but a configured entry uses shell:true with a raw shell string instead of {command,args}, so the parsed pinned command never matches and the override is silently never picked up for shell-style config entries.
preMortem.trigger: A future validate.commands[] entry is authored using the raw shell-string shorthand instead of the structured {command,args} object form.
preMortem.consequence: That command's evidence-pinning path silently falls back to the 270s default forever, reproducing this exact bug for a different config shape.
preMortem.mitigation: Pinned verification commands are always allowlisted executable+args per parseAllowlistedCommand and can never be shell-style by construction, so this cannot occur for the evidence-pinning path itself; CHK-003's regression coverage documents this as an intentional non-match, not a gap.

preMortem.scenario: Two configured validate.commands[] entries parse to the identical {executable,args} pair (e.g. a copy-pasted config edit) but carry different timeoutMs values.
preMortem.trigger: A future lattice.config.json edit duplicates a command with a changed timeoutMs but leaves the old entry in place.
preMortem.consequence: The matcher picks whichever entry appears first in the array, non-deterministically from the config author's perspective, silently applying the wrong budget.
preMortem.mitigation: Matching uses the first array match deterministically; documented as a config-authoring constraint (no duplicate {command,args} entries with different timeoutMs) rather than something the runtime needs to detect for this story.

preMortem.scenario: configuredValidationCommands(root) reads and parses lattice.config.json on every runSingleAllowlistedCommand invocation, adding I/O to a path already called once per checklist item during evidence recording.
preMortem.trigger: A story with many checklist items pins many different commands within one verification_evidence_batch_add call.
preMortem.consequence: Negligible in practice (one small local JSON read, no network) but could read as unnecessary repeated I/O in review.
preMortem.mitigation: No caching added given the file is small and local; noted as a possible follow-up only if it becomes a measured concern, not required for this story.

preMortem.scenario: quorum-submit-smoke.ts already carries its own --grep argv filter from B-3144 as a workaround; after this fix lands, a future story or agent might remove that filter believing it's now redundant.
preMortem.trigger: A later cleanup pass sees the timeout bug fixed and assumes the --grep workaround is now unnecessary.
preMortem.consequence: Evidence recording for that command becomes slower (356-360s per call) even though nothing forces it - not a correctness regression, just an avoidable slowdown and a wasted B-3144 optimization.
preMortem.mitigation: scope-boundary.json already excludes touching quorum-submit-smoke.ts's --grep mechanism in this story; both mechanisms are complementary (fast targeted runs via --grep, correct budget honoring for full runs) and neither supersedes the other.
